title: C#
description: Write your first programs in C#, the language of Unity and .NET: variables, loops, methods, collections, classes and modern null-safe C#, from zero.
keyIdeas: Every variable has a fixed type, and types decide what operators do: `7 / 2` is `3`, `7 / 2.0` is `3.5`.
Loop with `foreach`, keep things in a `List<T>` or a `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`, and query them with LINQ (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`).
Classes bundle data and behaviour; properties control who may change the data, and `static` members belong to the class itself.
Classes are reference types (assignment shares one object); `int`, structs and enums are value types (assignment copies).
Mark what may be missing with `?` and deal with it using `?.`, `??` or a null check before you use it.
Catch specific exceptions for real failures; use `TryParse`-style methods when bad input is expected.

concepts.label: Variables & static types
concepts.summary: A variable has a fixed type (int, double, float, bool, string) checked by the compiler; var only lets the compiler infer it.

concepts.label: String interpolation
concepts.summary: A $"..." string evaluates each {expression} and inserts its value, avoiding the left-to-right surprises of + concatenation.

concepts.label: Integer vs float division
concepts.summary: Operators follow precedence, and int / int drops the fraction, so one operand must be a double (or a cast) to keep it.

concepts.label: if and switch
concepts.summary: An if/else if chain runs the first branch whose bool condition is true; switch matches one value against cases, and a switch expression produces a value.

concepts.label: Loops
concepts.summary: while repeats until a condition changes, for counts with an index, foreach visits every item; break leaves and continue skips a round.

concepts.label: Methods & parameters
concepts.summary: A method has a return type, a name and typed parameters that receive copies of the arguments; every path must return a value unless it is void.

concepts.label: Arrays & List<T>
concepts.summary: An array has a fixed Length; a List<T> grows with Add and has a Count; both are indexed from 0 and hold one element type.

concepts.label: Dictionary<TKey, TValue>
concepts.summary: A dictionary maps unique keys to values for fast lookup; indexing a missing key throws, so use TryGetValue or GetValueOrDefault.

concepts.label: Lambdas & Func
concepts.summary: A lambda such as x => x * 2 is an inline function, stored in delegate types like Func<int, int> or Action<string>.

concepts.label: LINQ
concepts.summary: LINQ methods such as Where, Select, OrderBy and Count chain lambdas to filter, transform and sort collections; queries run when enumerated.

concepts.label: Classes, objects & constructors
concepts.summary: A class is a blueprint of fields and methods; new runs a constructor to create an object, and each object has its own state.

concepts.label: Properties
concepts.summary: A property reads like a field but runs a getter and setter, so { get; private set; }, init and computed => properties control access to state.

concepts.label: Structs, values & references
concepts.summary: Assigning or passing a value type (int, struct) copies it; a reference type (class, array, List) is shared, so changes show through every reference.

concepts.label: static members
concepts.summary: A static member belongs to the class itself and is shared by all objects; it cannot use instance fields without an object.

concepts.label: Inheritance & override
concepts.summary: A class can extend one base class, inheriting its members and replacing virtual methods with override; base calls the parent version.

concepts.label: Interfaces
concepts.summary: An interface is a contract of members that any class can implement (several per class), letting code depend on a capability rather than a concrete class.

concepts.label: Enums
concepts.summary: An enum is a value type of named constants backed by integers, ideal for a fixed set of states in a switch.

concepts.label: Records
concepts.summary: A record declares an immutable data type in one line with value equality, a readable ToString and with-expressions for modified copies.

concepts.label: Pattern matching
concepts.summary: is and switch expressions test a value against type, property and relational patterns, binding variables when they match.

concepts.label: Nullable reference types
concepts.summary: With nullable analysis on, string can never be null and string? may be, and the compiler warns (CS8602) before you dereference a maybe-null value.

concepts.label: ?. and ??
concepts.summary: a?.B gives null instead of crashing when a is null, x ?? y supplies a fallback, and ??= assigns only when the variable is null.

concepts.label: Exceptions
concepts.summary: Errors at run time throw exceptions that unwind until a matching catch; finally always runs, and TryParse avoids exceptions for expected bad input.

concepts.label: Delegates & events
concepts.summary: A delegate holds one or more methods to call; an event exposes one so outsiders can only subscribe with += and unsubscribe with -=, while the owner invokes it.

units.title: First programs
units.description: Variables, numbers, decisions, loops and methods: the building blocks of every C# program.

lessons.title: Your first program: values and variables
lessons.takeaway: A variable has a name, a type and a value; the value can change but the type never does, and `$"...{expr}..."` puts values into text.

steps.title: A program is a list of instructions
steps.body:
A program is a list of instructions that the computer runs **from top to bottom**. In C#, each instruction (a *statement*) ends with a semicolon.

```csharp
Console.WriteLine("Hello, world!");   // prints a line of text
Console.WriteLine(2 + 3);             // prints 5
// Lines starting with // are comments: C# skips them.
```

`Console.WriteLine(...)` prints whatever is in the brackets and moves to a new line. Text goes in double quotes; `2 + 3` without quotes is a calculation, so it prints `5`.

Modern C# lets a file start straight away with statements like these (*top-level statements*). Older tutorials wrap the same lines in `class Program { static void Main() { ... } }`; it means the same thing.

steps.title: Variables have a type
steps.body:
A **variable** is a named place to keep a value. You declare it with a **type**, a name and a starting value:

```csharp
int lives = 3;              // a whole number
double speed = 4.5;         // a number with a fraction
bool paused = false;        // true or false
string name = "Ana";        // text, in double quotes
var level = 1;              // var: the compiler works out that level is an int

lives = lives - 1;          // a variable can change its value...
Console.WriteLine(lives);   // prints 2
// lives = "two";           // ...but never its type: this line would not compile
Console.WriteLine($"{speed} {paused} {name} {level}");
```

The everyday types: `int` for whole numbers, `double` for numbers with a fraction, `bool` for `true`/`false` and `string` for text. C# is **statically typed**: a variable's type is fixed when you declare it, and the compiler rejects a value of the wrong type *before the program runs*. `var` doesn't change that; it only lets the compiler fill in the type from the starting value.

steps.prompt: Each line runs in order, and `=` stores a new value. What does this print?
steps.hint: `coins = coins + 2` reads the current value, adds 2 and stores the result back.
steps.explanation: `coins` starts at 3, becomes 3 + 2 = 5, then 5 × 2 = **10**. The last line prints the text `"coins"`, not the variable: anything in double quotes is a string, printed exactly as written.

steps.title: Putting values into text
steps.body:
To build a message from values, put a `$` in front of the string and write any expression inside `{ }`. This is **string interpolation**, and it's the usual way to format output:

```csharp
string name = "Ana";
int score = 42;
Console.WriteLine("Hi " + name + "!");               // Hi Ana!
Console.WriteLine($"{name} scored {score} points");  // Ana scored 42 points
Console.WriteLine($"Double: {score * 2}");           // Double: 84
```

`+` also joins strings, and it turns a number into text when one side is a string. That's handy, but it runs **left to right**, which can surprise you, as the next questions show.

steps.title: A shop receipt
steps.problem: You have `string item = "Potion";`, `int price = 4;` and `int count = 3;`. Write one line that prints `3 x Potion = 12 coins`. Try it before revealing the steps.
steps: Start with an interpolated string: `$"..."`. Everything outside braces is printed as written.
The count and the item name go straight in: `{count} x {item}`.
The total isn't stored anywhere, but braces take any expression, so compute it inline: `{count * price}`.
steps.answer: `Console.WriteLine($"{count} x {item} = {count * price} coins");` prints `3 x Potion = 12 coins`.

steps.prompt: Two ways to print a total. What does this print?
steps.hint: `+` works left to right. What is `"Total: " + 2`: a number or a string?
steps.explanation: `"Total: " + a` is a string, `"Total: 2"`, so the next `+ b` glues on `3` as text: **Total: 23**. In the interpolated string, `{a + b}` is computed first as numbers, giving **Total: 5**. Interpolation avoids the trap; with `+` you'd need brackets: `"Total: " + (a + b)`.

steps.prompt: This should print `Lives: 4`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0029: Cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'int'
steps.hint: What type did line 1 give `lives`, and what type is `"4"`?
steps.explanation: `lives` is an `int`, and `"4"` (in quotes) is a `string`, so the compiler stops with **CS0029**. Store the number `4` instead. `var lives = 3` still makes `lives` an `int`; `var lives = "4"` tries to declare a second variable with the same name (CS0128); and line 4 never gets a chance to run.

steps.prompt: Pick the best type for each value in a small game.

items.text: Number of lives left
How many enemies are on screen
A lap time in seconds, like 12.84
The average score, like 7.5
Is the game paused?
Whether the door is locked
The player's name
A message to show on screen

steps.explanation: Counts of whole things are `int`. Measurements that can have a fraction are `double`. Yes/no questions are `bool`. Text of any kind, even a single word, is a `string`.

lessons.title: Numbers, operators and division
lessons.takeaway: `int / int` is an `int` (7 / 2 is 3, the fraction is dropped), so make one side a `double` (7 / 2.0) when you want 3.5.

steps.title: Arithmetic
steps.body:
C# has the operators you'd expect: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, plus `%` for the **remainder** after division. `*`, `/` and `%` go before `+` and `-`; brackets go first of all.

```csharp
int a = 7 + 3 * 2;       // 13: * and / happen before + and -
int b = (7 + 3) * 2;     // 20: parentheses go first
int c = 17 % 5;          // 2: the remainder of 17 / 5

int score = 10;
score += 5;              // same as score = score + 5, so 15
score *= 2;              // 30
score++;                 // add 1: 31
Console.WriteLine($"{a} {b} {c} {score}");   // 13 20 2 31
```

`score += 5` is short for `score = score + 5`; there are `-=`, `*=`, `/=` and `%=` too. `score++` adds one and `score--` subtracts one.

steps.title: Integer division drops the fraction
steps.body:
The types of the two sides decide what `/` does. If **both** are `int`, the result is an `int` and the fraction is simply dropped (not rounded). If **either** is a `double`, you get a `double`.

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2);          // 3    int / int gives an int: the fraction is dropped
Console.WriteLine(7 / 2.0);        // 3.5  one double makes it a double division
Console.WriteLine((double)7 / 2);  // 3.5  the cast turns 7 into a double first
Console.WriteLine((int)3.9);       // 3    casting to int cuts the fraction off

float speed = 2.5f;                // a float literal needs an f on the end
Console.WriteLine(speed * 2);      // 5
```

`(double)` and `(int)` are **casts**: they convert a value to another type. `float` is a smaller, less precise `double`; game engines such as Unity use it everywhere, and its literals need an `f`: `2.5f`.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Integer division drops the fraction. Which way does -3.5 go when you just drop the .5?
steps.explanation: `7 / 2` is `int / int`, so **3**. `7 / 2.0` involves a `double`, so **3.5**. `7 % 2` is the remainder, **1**. `-7 / 2` is -3.5 with the fraction dropped, which is **-3**: C# cuts toward zero. (Python's `//` would give -4, because it rounds down.)

steps.title: An average that comes out wrong
steps.problem: Three scores add up to `int sum = 14;`. The code `double avg = sum / 3;` stores `4`, even though `avg` is a `double`. Why, and how do you get 4.67?
steps: The right-hand side is worked out first: `sum / 3` is `int / int`, which is the `int` 4.
Only then is 4 stored in the `double`, as `4`. The fraction was already gone, so the variable's type is too late to help.
Make one side of the division a `double`: `sum / 3.0` (or `(double)sum / 3`) gives `4.666666666666667`.
To show two decimals, round when you display it: `Math.Round(avg, 2)` gives `4.67`.
steps.answer: `double avg = sum / 3.0;` stores 4.666666666666667, and `Math.Round(avg, 2)` gives 4.67. What decides the division is the type of the operands, not the type of the variable you store the result in.

steps.hint: Work left to right: what is `30 / 40` in integer division?
steps.explanation: `collected / total` is `30 / 40`, an integer division, so it's **0**, and 0 × 100 is still 0. Multiply first and the problem disappears: `collected * 100 / total` is `3000 / 40`, which is 75.

steps.prompt: This should print `3.5`. Click the line with the bug.
steps.hint: When is the fraction lost: during the division, or when the result is stored?
steps.explanation: `total / count` is `int / int`, so it's 3 before it ever reaches `average`. Casting `total` to `double` **before** dividing makes it a `double` division: 3.5. `(double)(total / count)` divides first and converts the 3 afterwards; casting `average` when printing is too late; and `int total = 7.0` doesn't compile (CS0266: a `double` won't fit in an `int` without a cast).

steps.prompt: Unity code uses `float` everywhere. This should print `10`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0664: Literal of type double cannot be implicitly converted to type 'float'; use an 'F' suffix to create a literal of this type
steps.hint: A number with a decimal point, written on its own, is a `double`.
steps.explanation: `2.5` is a `double` literal, and C# won't silently squeeze a `double` into a smaller `float`, so it asks for an `F` suffix (CS0664). `4` is fine: an `int` converts to `float` automatically. `(int)2.5` compiles but stores 2, so it prints 8. And C# always uses a dot for decimals; `2,5` is a syntax error.

steps.prompt: Step through and predict `hp` and `bonus` when asked.
steps.hint: `hp *= 2` means `hp = hp * 2`. `18 / 4` is integer division.
steps.explanation: `hp` goes 10 → 7 → **14**. `14 % 5` is the remainder after taking out two fives, **4**. Adding the bonus gives 18, and `18 / 4` in integer division is **4** (4.5 with the fraction dropped).

frames.note: Integer division again: the fraction is dropped.

lessons.title: Decisions: if and switch
lessons.takeaway: An `if`/`else if` chain runs only the first branch whose condition is true, and a `switch` expression picks a value by matching cases, with `_` for everything else.

steps.title: if, else if, else

steps.prompt: Ana scored 85. What does this print?
steps.hint: Which condition is checked first, and is it true for 85?
steps.explanation: 85 >= 50 is true, so the first block runs and the rest of the chain is skipped: **pass**. The `>= 80` branch can never run, because every score that reaches it was already caught by `>= 50`. Put the strictest test first: `>= 80`, then `>= 50`.

steps.title: Combining conditions
steps.body:
`&&` means **and**, `||` means **or**, and `!` means **not**. For a choice between two values, the conditional operator `condition ? a : b` is a compact `if`/`else`:

```csharp
int age = 15;
bool hasTicket = true;

bool canEnter = age >= 12 && hasTicket;          // true: both sides are true
bool discount = age < 12 || age >= 65;           // false: neither side is true
string label = canEnter ? "Welcome" : "Sorry";   // condition ? value if true : value if false

Console.WriteLine($"{canEnter} {discount} {label}");   // True False Welcome
```

`&&` and `||` stop as soon as the answer is known: in `a && b`, if `a` is false, `b` is never evaluated.

steps.prompt: This should print `Game over`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0029: Cannot implicitly convert type 'int' to 'bool'
steps.hint: Is `lives = 0` a question or an instruction?
steps.explanation: `lives = 0` **stores** 0 and its value is the `int` 0, but `if` needs a `bool`, so the compiler refuses (CS0029). `==` asks the question. C# has no `===` (that's JavaScript), `bool lives = 0` can't hold a number, and `lives = false` tries to store a `bool` in an `int`.

steps.title: switch

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: With `roll` 6 the second arm matches: **critical**. After `roll = 3`, neither 1 nor 6 matches, so `_` supplies **hit**. A switch expression can sit anywhere a value can, even inside `Console.WriteLine(...)`.

steps.title: Ticket prices
steps.problem: Children under 12 pay 5 coins, people aged 65 or over pay 7, everyone else pays 10. Write the `if` chain, then work out what ages 12, 64 and 65 pay.
steps: One branch per rule, with the catch-all last: `if (age < 12) price = 5; else if (age >= 65) price = 7; else price = 10;`
Age 12: `12 < 12` is false and `12 >= 65` is false, so `else`: 10.
Age 64: both tests are false: 10.
Age 65: `65 >= 65` is true: 7. The boundaries are where bugs hide, so always test the exact values 12 and 65.

steps.hint: Work out `damage` first, then decide which branch of the `if` runs.
steps.explanation: `shielded` is true, so `damage` is 1. `hp - damage` is 3, which isn't `<= 0`, and `!shielded` is false, so the `||` is false and the `else` runs: `hp -= 1 * 2` leaves **2**.

lessons.title: Loops: while, for and foreach
lessons.takeaway: Use `foreach` to visit every item, `for` when you need the index or a count, and `while` to repeat until a condition changes; indexes run from 0 to Length - 1.

steps.title: while and for

steps.prompt: Step through the loop and predict `total` when asked.
steps.hint: Each round adds `i * i`: 1, then 4, then 9, then 16.
steps.explanation: `total` collects the squares: 0 + 1 = 1, + 4 = **5**, + 9 = **14**, + 16 = **30**. The variable `i` only exists inside the `for`, so the last frame no longer shows it.

frames.note: First round: i is 1, so total gains `1 * 1`.
After this round `i++` makes i 5, `i <= 4` is false and the loop ends.

steps.title: foreach, break and continue
steps.body:
`foreach` visits every item of a collection, such as an **array**, without any index arithmetic:

```csharp
string[] names = { "Ana", "Ben", "Cy" };   // an array: a fixed row of values

foreach (string name in names)             // name takes each value in turn
{
    if (name == "Ben") continue;           // skip the rest of this round
    Console.WriteLine($"Hi {name}");       // Hi Ana, then Hi Cy
}
```

`continue` jumps to the next round; `break` leaves the loop completely. An array's items are numbered from **0**, so a 3-item array has indexes 0, 1 and 2, and `names.Length` is 3.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: A 6 skips just that round. A 1 ends the whole loop.
steps.explanation: 3 is printed. The first 6 hits `continue`, so nothing is printed for it. 2 is printed. The second 6 is skipped too. Then 1 hits `break`, and the loop ends before it ever reaches 5.

steps.prompt: This should add up the scores and print `20`, but it crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
Unhandled exception. System.IndexOutOfRangeException: Index was outside the bounds of the array.
  ...
fixes: Change line 3 to `for (int i = 0; i < scores.Length; i++)`
Change line 3 to `for (int i = 1; i <= scores.Length; i++)`
Change line 3 to `for (int i = 0; i <= scores.Length - 2; i++)`
steps.hint: `scores.Length` is 3. Which indexes exist?
steps.explanation: The valid indexes are 0, 1 and 2, but `i <= scores.Length` also runs with `i = 3`, so `scores[3]` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`. Use `<`. Starting at 1 still reaches 3; `scores[i - 1]` asks for index -1 on the first round; and stopping at `Length - 2` skips the last score and prints 16. Even simpler: `foreach (int s in scores) sum += s;` can't get the bounds wrong.

steps.hint: Write down `n` after each round: 100, 50, 25, ... and remember integer division.
steps.explanation: `n` goes 100 → 50 → 25 → 12 → 6 → 3 → 1: **6** rounds. 25 / 2 is 12 and 3 / 2 is 1, because integer division drops the fraction. When `n` reaches 1, `n > 1` is false and the loop stops.

steps.prompt: Which loop fits each job best?

items.text: Print every name in an array
Add up all the prices in a list
Count down from 10 to 1
Do something with every second item, using its index
Ask again until the player types a valid number
Keep halving a value until it drops below 1

steps.explanation: `foreach` is for visiting every item when you don't need the index. `for` is for counting, or when the index itself matters. `while` is for repeating until something changes and you don't know in advance how many rounds that takes.

lessons.title: Methods: name a piece of work
lessons.takeaway: A method has a return type, a name and typed parameters; it gets copies of the values you pass in, and every path through it must `return` a value unless it's `void`.

steps.title: Define once, call many times

steps.prompt: Calls inside calls run from the inside out. What does this print?
steps.hint: Evaluate the innermost call first, then pass its result outward.
steps.explanation: `Add(2, 3)` is 5 and `Twice(5)` is **10**. In the second line `Twice(2)` is 4 and `Add(4, 3)` is **7**. `=> a + b` is the short form of a method body: `{ return a + b; }`.

steps.title: Parameters, defaults and names
steps.body:
A parameter can have a **default value**, used when the caller leaves it out. A caller can also name an argument, which makes calls easier to read:

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(Damage(5));                  // 5: multiplier uses its default, 1
Console.WriteLine(Damage(5, 3));               // 15
Console.WriteLine(Damage(5, multiplier: 2));   // 10: a named argument

int Damage(int baseDamage, int multiplier = 1) => baseDamage * multiplier;
```

When you pass an `int` (or a `double`, a `bool`...), the method gets a **copy** of the value. Changing the parameter inside the method doesn't touch the caller's variable.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: `amount` is a copy of `gold`, not another name for it.
steps.explanation: `Spend` receives a copy of 10 in `amount`, sets that copy to 0 and prints **0**. Back outside, `gold` is untouched: **10**. To change the caller's value, return the new value and assign it: `gold = Spend(gold);`.

steps.prompt: `Grade` should give `"C"` for anything below 70, so this should print `B`. It doesn't compile. Click the line where the fix belongs.
steps.error: error CS0161: 'Grade(int)': not all code paths return a value
fixes: Add `return "C";` on a new line just before line 9
steps.hint: What does `Grade(50)` return?
steps.explanation: A score below 70 falls through both `if`s and reaches the closing brace with nothing to return, so the compiler rejects the method (CS0161), whatever value you actually call it with. Add a final `return "C";`. A `void` method can't return `"A"`; `else if` still leaves the same path uncovered; and changing the call doesn't change the method.

steps.title: Write your own
steps.problem: Write a method `IsEven` that takes an `int` and tells you whether it's even. Then use it in a loop to count the even numbers from 1 to 10. Try writing it before you reveal the steps.
steps: The answer is yes or no, so the return type is `bool`: `bool IsEven(int n)`.
A number is even when the remainder after dividing by 2 is 0, and `n % 2 == 0` is already a `bool`, so return it directly: `bool IsEven(int n) => n % 2 == 0;`
Loop over 1 to 10 and count the hits: `for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++) { if (IsEven(i)) evens++; }`
steps.answer: `evens` ends at 5 (2, 4, 6, 8, 10). Returning `n % 2 == 0` directly is cleaner than `if (n % 2 == 0) return true; else return false;`.

steps.hint: Work out each call separately. Which parameters keep their defaults in the last one?
steps.explanation: `Clamp(150)` uses the defaults 0 and 100, so it returns 100. `Clamp(-5)` returns 0. `Clamp(42, max: 40)` keeps `min` at 0 but sets `max` to 40, so it returns 40. The total is **140**.

units.title: Collections and LINQ
units.description: Keep many values together, look them up by key, and filter and sort them in one line.

lessons.title: Arrays and List<T>
lessons.takeaway: An array has a fixed `Length`; a `List<T>` grows with `Add` and has a `Count`; both start at index 0, and you can't assign to an index that doesn't exist yet.

steps.title: Arrays: a fixed row of values
steps.body:
An **array** holds a fixed number of values of one type. `int[]` means "array of `int`". You reach an item by its **index**, starting at 0:

```csharp
int[] scores = { 7, 9, 4 };        // an array of 3 ints
Console.WriteLine(scores[0]);      // 7: the first item is at index 0
Console.WriteLine(scores.Length);  // 3
scores[2] = 10;                    // replace the last item

int[] empty = new int[5];          // 5 ints, each starting at 0
Console.WriteLine(empty[1] + scores[2]);   // 10
Console.WriteLine(empty.Length);   // 5: the size is fixed when the array is made
```

The size is set when the array is created and never changes. Reading or writing outside 0 to `Length - 1` throws `IndexOutOfRangeException`.

steps.title: List<T>: a row that grows
steps.body:
Most of the time you don't know the size in advance, so you use a **`List<T>`**. The `T` in angle brackets is the item type: a `List<string>` holds only strings. This is called **generics**, and you'll see it again in `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`.

```csharp
var names = new List<string> { "Ana", "Ben" };   // a list that holds strings
names.Add("Cy");                   // grows: Ana, Ben, Cy
names.Remove("Ana");               // shrinks: Ben, Cy
Console.WriteLine(names.Count);    // 2
Console.WriteLine(names[0]);       // Ben
Console.WriteLine(names.Contains("Cy"));   // True

List<int> numbers = [3, 1, 2];     // the newer [ ] syntax works too
numbers.Sort();
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", numbers));   // 1, 2, 3
```

Arrays use `Length`, lists use `Count`. `string.Join(", ", list)` is a quick way to print every item.

steps.prompt: Step through and predict the list when asked. Watch the difference between `Remove` and `RemoveAt`.
steps.hint: `Remove(2)` looks for the **value** 2. `RemoveAt(0)` removes whatever is at **index** 0.
steps.explanation: `Add` appends 2 at the end and `Insert(0, 9)` puts 9 at the front: **[9, 4, 7, 2]**. `Remove(2)` searches for the value 2, not index 2, so the last item goes: **[9, 4, 7]**. `RemoveAt(0)` removes the item at index 0, the 9: **[4, 7]**. `Count` is 2 and the program prints `4 2`.

frames.note: `Insert(0, ...)` puts the new item at the front and shifts the rest along.
`RemoveAt` takes out the item at an index.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: `new int[3]` makes three items straight away. A new list starts empty.
steps.explanation: `new int[3]` creates three ints, all 0, so `Length` is **3** even though only one was set. The list starts empty and has one item after `Add`, so `Count` is **1**. `a[0] + a[1]` is 0 + 5 = **5**.

steps.prompt: This should print `sword, shield`, but it crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
Unhandled exception. System.ArgumentOutOfRangeException: Index was out of range. Must be non-negative and less than the size of the collection. (Parameter 'index')
  ...
fixes: Change line 1 to `var items = new List<string>(2);`
Change line 1 to `var items = new string[2];`
steps.hint: How many items does the list have when line 2 runs?
steps.explanation: A new list is empty, so index 0 doesn't exist yet and `items[0] = ...` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`. An index can only replace an item that's already there; `Add` creates new ones. `new List<string>(2)` only reserves room (the *capacity*): `Count` is still 0. `items[1]` is just as missing. An array has no `Add` method, so line 3 wouldn't compile.

steps.title: The highest score
steps.problem: `var scores = new List<int> { 12, 40, 7, 33 };` Find the highest score with a loop. Decide what `best` should start as before you reveal the steps.
steps: Start with a real item, not 0: `int best = scores[0];` (if every score were negative, 0 would be wrong).
Visit every score: `foreach (int s in scores)`.
Keep the larger one: `if (s > best) best = s;`. After the loop, `best` is 40.
This job is so common that C# has it built in: `scores.Max()` also gives 40. The next lesson shows that family of methods.
steps.answer: `best` is 40. The pattern is: start with the first item, compare every item, keep the winner.

steps.prompt: Array or `List<T>`? Sort each collection by the best fit.

items.text: The 64 squares of a chess board
The 7 days of the week
Red, green and blue parts of a colour
Items the player picks up during a level
Chat messages as they arrive
Enemies spawned and destroyed during play

steps.explanation: An array suits data whose size is known and never changes: board squares, weekdays, colour parts. A `List<T>` suits anything that grows or shrinks as the program runs. When in doubt, start with a `List<T>`.

lessons.title: Dictionaries: look things up by key
lessons.takeaway: A `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` maps each unique key to a value; `dict[key] = value` adds or replaces, and `TryGetValue` or `GetValueOrDefault` handle missing keys without crashing.

steps.title: A dictionary maps keys to values

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: Assigning to `"apple"` a second time: new entry, or replacement?
steps.explanation: Keys are unique, so the second `stock["apple"] = 5` **replaces** 3 instead of adding an entry. There are **2** keys, apple and pear, and apple's value is **5**.

steps.title: When the key isn't there
Counting words
steps.problem: Count how often each word appears in `"red blue red green red"`. How many times does `red` appear, and how many entries does the dictionary end with? Plan it before you reveal the steps.
steps: Split the text into words: `text.Split(' ')` gives an array of 5 strings.
Use the word as the key and its count as the value: `var counts = new Dictionary<string, int>();`
For each word, take the current count (0 the first time) and add 1: `counts[word] = counts.GetValueOrDefault(word) + 1;`
red is counted 3 times, blue once, green once.
steps.answer: `counts["red"]` is 3 and `counts.Count` is 3 (red, blue, green). `GetValueOrDefault` is what makes the first sighting of each word work.

steps.prompt: Step through the counting loop and predict `seen` when asked.
steps.hint: `seen` is whatever is stored for the current word so far, or 0 for a word that isn't a key yet.
steps.explanation: The first `red` is missing, so `seen` is 0 and red gets 1. `blue` is new as well: `seen` is **0** again. The second `red` finds the 1 stored earlier, so `seen` is **1** and red becomes 2. The program prints 2.

frames.note: "red" isn't a key yet, so `GetValueOrDefault` gives 0.
The second red found 1 and stored 2.

steps.prompt: This should print `Cy is unknown`, but it crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
Unhandled exception. System.Collections.Generic.KeyNotFoundException: The given key 'Cy' was not present in the dictionary.
  ...
steps.hint: Cy isn't one of the keys. Which method copes with a missing key and gives back an `int`?
steps.explanation: `ages["Cy"]` throws `KeyNotFoundException` because Cy isn't a key. `GetValueOrDefault` returns 0 instead, and line 4 then prints `Cy is unknown`. `ContainsKey` returns a `bool`, not an age; `??` only works on values that can be null, and an `int` can't (CS0019); and `TryGetValue` needs a second `out` argument to put the value in.

steps.prompt: `List<T>` or `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>`? Sort each job.

items.text: The moves made so far, in order
The cards in a hand, left to right
The top ten scores, best first
A player's score, found by their name
Item ids mapped to item names
How often each word appears

steps.explanation: Use a list when **order** matters and you go through the items one after another. Use a dictionary when you **look things up** by something other than position: a name, an id, a word.

lessons.title: Lambdas and LINQ
lessons.takeaway: A lambda like `x => x * 2` is a small inline function; LINQ chains them to filter (`Where`), transform (`Select`) and sort (`OrderBy`), and a query runs only when you loop over it or call `ToList`.

steps.title: Functions as values
steps.body:
A **lambda** is a small function without a name: parameters, an arrow `=>`, and the result. You can store one in a variable, typed as a **`Func`** (returns a value) or an **`Action`** (returns nothing):

```csharp
Func<int, int> twice = x => x * 2;           // takes an int, returns an int
Func<int, int, int> add = (a, b) => a + b;   // two ints in, one int out
Func<string, bool> isLong = s => s.Length > 5;
Action<string> shout = s => Console.WriteLine(s.ToUpper());   // Action: returns nothing

Console.WriteLine(twice(21));         // 42
Console.WriteLine(add(2, 3));         // 5
Console.WriteLine(isLong("hello"));   // False
shout("hi");                          // HI
```

In `Func<int, bool>` the last type is what the function returns; the ones before it are the parameters. You'll rarely write these types yourself, but you'll pass lambdas to methods all the time.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.explanation: `twice(7)` is **14**. `twice(4)` is 8, and `isBig(8)` checks 8 > 10, which is **False**. Calling a lambda looks exactly like calling a method.

steps.title: LINQ: queries over collections
steps.body:
**LINQ** is a set of methods on every array and list that take a lambda and do a common loop for you:

```csharp
var scores = new List<int> { 72, 95, 40, 88 };

var passed = scores.Where(s => s >= 50);         // keep items where the lambda is true
var curved = scores.Select(s => s + 5);          // turn each item into a new value
var ranked = scores.OrderByDescending(s => s);   // sort by a key, highest first

Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", passed));    // 72, 95, 88
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", curved));    // 77, 100, 45, 93
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", ranked));    // 95, 88, 72, 40
Console.WriteLine($"{scores.Count(s => s > 80)} {scores.Sum()} {scores.Max()}");   // 2 295 95
```

`Where`, `Select` and `OrderBy` return a new sequence and leave the original list untouched, so you can **chain** them: `.Where(...).OrderBy(...).Select(...)`. Add `.ToList()` at the end to get a real `List<T>`.

steps.prompt: Follow the chain one method at a time. What does this print?
steps.hint: Filter, then sort, then turn each score into `s / 10` (integer division).
steps.explanation: `Where` keeps 72, 95, 88 and 61. `OrderByDescending` sorts them: 95, 88, 72, 61. `Select(s => s / 10)` uses integer division: **9, 8, 7, 6**. `Count(s => s < 60)` counts the scores under 60 in the original array: just 40, so **1**.

steps.title: Reading a query
steps.problem: `string[] names = { "ana", "Ben", "cy", "Dee" };` What does `names.Where(n => char.IsUpper(n[0])).Select(n => n.ToUpper()).ToList()` contain? Work through it before revealing the steps.
steps: Read it left to right, one stage at a time. `n[0]` is a string's first character.
`Where` keeps the names whose first letter is upper case: "Ben" and "Dee".
`Select` turns each one into its upper-case version: "BEN", "DEE".
`ToList()` collects the result into a new `List<string>`; `names` itself is unchanged.
steps.answer: A list holding `BEN` and `DEE`. The same with loops would need an empty list, a `foreach`, an `if` and an `Add`.

steps.prompt: This should print the prices under 10: `4.5, 3.25`. Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 2 to `var cheap = prices.Where(p => p < 10);`
Change line 2 to `var cheap = prices.Select(p => p < 10).ToList();`
Change line 2 to `var cheap = prices.OrderBy(p => p < 10);`
steps.hint: `Select` transforms every item. Which method keeps or drops items?
steps.explanation: `Select` turns **every** price into the result of the lambda, here a `bool`, so it prints `True, False, True, False`. `Where` uses the lambda as a test and keeps the prices that pass. `ToList()` doesn't change what `Select` produced; `OrderBy` sorts by the test (false first) but keeps all four; and printing the query directly shows its type name, not its items.

steps.title: Queries run late
steps.body:
A LINQ query like `nums.Where(...)` is a **recipe**, not a result. It runs each time you loop over it or call something like `Count()` or `ToList()`, and it uses the collection as it is *at that moment*. This is called **deferred execution**:

```csharp
var nums = new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 };
var odd = nums.Where(n => n % 2 == 1);   // nothing has been filtered yet
nums.Add(5);
Console.WriteLine(odd.Count());          // 3: the query runs now and sees 1, 3 and 5
```

When you want a fixed snapshot, call `.ToList()` (or `.ToArray()`) once and keep the result.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: `big` is a recipe; `snapshot` is a list built from it before 4 was added.
steps.explanation: `ToList()` ran the query straight away, so `snapshot` holds 2 and 3: **2** items. `big` runs again when `Count()` is called, after 4 was added, so it finds 2, 3 and 4: **3**.

units.title: Objects and types
units.description: Model things as classes, control their data with properties, and know when a value is copied or shared.

lessons.title: Classes, objects and constructors
lessons.takeaway: A class is a blueprint, `new` runs its constructor to build an object with its own state, and properties like `{ get; private set; }` decide who may change that state.

steps.title: A class is a blueprint

steps.prompt: Two objects from the same class. What does this print?
steps.hint: Each `new Counter()` gets its own `Count` field.
steps.explanation: Every object has its own copy of the fields. `a` was incremented twice and `b` once, so it prints **2 1**. The class is the blueprint; `a` and `b` are two separate things built from it.

steps.prompt: This should print `Ana`, but it prints an empty line. Click the line with the bug.
fixes: Change line 8 to `public void Player(string name)`
Change line 1 to `var p = new Player(name: "Ana");`
steps.hint: `=` copies from the right-hand side into the left-hand side. Which one is the field?
steps.explanation: `name = Name` copies the field (still `""`) **into the parameter**, the wrong way round, so the field never changes. `Name = name` stores the argument in the field. Removing the `= ""` just leaves the field null; a constructor has no return type, so `void Player` turns it into an ordinary method (which C# rejects, since it has the class's name); and naming the argument changes nothing.

steps.title: Properties guard the data

steps.prompt: `Area` is a computed property. What does this print?
steps.hint: Is `Area` stored once, or worked out each time you read it?
steps.explanation: `Area => Width * Height` has no stored value; it runs each time it's read. First 2 × 3 = **6**. After `Width` changes to 5, reading it again gives 5 × 3 = **15**. A stored field would have gone stale.

items.text: `ship.Hit(10);`
`int h = ship.Hull;`
`Console.WriteLine(ship.Sunk);`
`var kite = new Ship { Name = "Kite" };`
`ship.Hull = 50;`
`ship.Sunk = true;`
`ship.Name = "Bolt";`

steps.hint: Reading is always allowed here. For each write, check the property's setter: public, private, init, or none at all?
steps.explanation: Reading `Hull` and `Sunk` and calling the public `Hit` are fine, and `init` allows setting `Name` while the object is being created. But `Hull`'s setter is private (CS0272), `Sunk` is computed and has no setter at all (CS0200), and an `init` property can't be changed after creation (CS8852). The only way to lower `Hull` from outside is `Hit`, which is exactly the point.

steps.title: Design a small class
steps.problem: Design a `CountdownTimer`: it starts with a number of seconds, `Tick()` takes one second off, and code outside can read how many seconds remain and whether it's done, but can't change the time directly. Sketch it before revealing the steps.
steps: The remaining time is data everyone may read but only the timer may change: `public int Remaining { get; private set; }`.
"Done" can be computed from it, so it shouldn't be stored separately: `public bool IsDone => Remaining <= 0;`
The constructor sets the starting time: `public CountdownTimer(int seconds) => Remaining = seconds;`
`Tick` is the only way to change it: `public void Tick() => Remaining--;`
steps.answer: With `new CountdownTimer(3)`, a `while (!t.IsDone) t.Tick();` loop runs 3 times and leaves `Remaining` at 0. Choosing what is stored, what is computed and who may write it is most of class design.

lessons.title: Value types, reference types and static
lessons.takeaway: Assigning or passing a class shares one object, while `int`, structs and enums are copied; `static` members belong to the class, so they're shared and can't touch instance fields.

steps.title: Copied or shared?
steps.body:
C# has two kinds of types, and they behave differently when you assign them or pass them to a method:

- **Value types** (`int`, `double`, `bool`, `char`, enums, structs) hold the data itself. `b = a` **copies** it.
- **Reference types** (classes, `string`, arrays, `List<T>`, `Dictionary`) live elsewhere and a variable holds a **reference** to them. `b = a` copies the reference, so `a` and `b` are two names for **one** object.

`string` is a reference type, but strings can never be changed, so in practice they behave like values.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: `List<int>` is a class. `int` is a value type.
steps.explanation: `var b = a` makes `b` refer to the same list, so `b.Add(3)` is visible through `a`: **3** items. `int y = x` copies the number, so `y++` changes only `y` and `x` is still **5**.

steps.title: Structs: your own value types

steps.prompt: `Point` is a struct and `Box` is a class, with the same field. Step through and predict the values.
steps.hint: How many `Point` values exist after line 2? How many `Box` objects after line 5?
steps.explanation: `p2 = p1` copies the whole struct, so changing `p2.X` leaves `p1.X` at **1**. `b2 = b1` copies a reference to the single `Box`, so `b2.X = 9` changes the object that `b1` refers to as well: `b1.X` is **9**. Same syntax, different behaviour, decided by `struct` or `class`.

frames.note: `b2 = b1` copies the reference: one Box, two names.

steps.prompt: `MoveRight` should move the point, so this should print `1`. It prints `0`. Click the line that makes `MoveRight` work on a copy.
fixes: Change line 10 to `class Point { public int X, Y; }`
Change line 5 to `void MoveRight(ref Point p)`
Change line 2 to `MoveRight(new Point { X = pos.X, Y = pos.Y });`
steps.hint: What kind of type is `Point`, and what does a method receive when you pass one?
steps.explanation: `Point` is a struct, so `MoveRight` receives a **copy**: it moves the copy and throws it away. As a class, the parameter refers to the same object and the change sticks. `p.X = p.X + 1` is the same change to the same copy. A `ref` parameter would work, but the call must say `ref` too (CS1620). Passing a brand-new `Point` copies even more. (With a struct, the usual style is to return the new value: `pos = MoveRight(pos);`.)

steps.title: static: belongs to the class
steps.body:
Normal (*instance*) members belong to each object. A **`static`** member belongs to the class itself: there's exactly one, shared by everyone, and you use it through the class name.

```csharp
Console.WriteLine(Math.Max(3, 8));    // 8: called on the class Math, no object needed
Console.WriteLine(Settings.Volume);   // 7

Settings.Volume = 10;                 // one value, shared by the whole program
Console.WriteLine(Settings.Volume);   // 10

static class Settings                 // a static class can't be created with new
{
    public static int Volume = 7;
}
```

You've been using static members all along: `Console.WriteLine`, `Math.Max`, `int.Parse`. A static method has no object to work on, so it **can't** use instance fields.

steps.prompt: `Count` is static and `Id` is not. What does this print?
steps.hint: There is one `Count` for the whole class, and each enemy copies its value into its own `Id` when it's created.
steps.explanation: All three constructors increment the **same** static `Count`, so it ends at **3**. Each enemy stores the count at the moment it was created in its own `Id`: `a` got 1, `b` got **2**, `c` got 3.

steps.prompt: This should print `6`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0120: An object reference is required for the non-static field, method, or property 'Dice.sides'
fixes: Change line 5 to `private static int sides = 6;`
Change line 6 to `public static int MaxRoll() => this.sides;`
steps.hint: `MaxRoll` is static: which object's `sides` would it read?
steps.explanation: A static method runs without any object, so there's no `sides` for it to read (CS0120). Making `sides` static too gives it one shared value. Calling it through `new Dice()` doesn't help: the method is still static and still can't see `sides`. There's no `this` in a static method (CS0026), and a static class can't contain instance fields (CS0708).

lessons.title: Inheritance, interfaces and enums
lessons.takeaway: A class inherits from one base class and replaces `virtual` methods with `override`; an interface is a promise any class can keep; an enum names a fixed set of states.

steps.title: Inheritance

steps.prompt: Every item in the array is typed as `Enemy`. What does this print?
steps.hint: With `virtual`/`override`, the object's real class decides which `Speak` runs, not the variable's type.
steps.explanation: The plain `Enemy` prints **...**. The Slime's override prints **blub**, even through a variable of type `Enemy`: this is *polymorphism*. The Bat calls `base.Speak()`, which gives `...`, and adds `squeak`: **...squeak**.

steps.title: Interfaces: a promise

steps.prompt: This should print `hit`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0535: 'Crate' does not implement interface member 'IDamageable.TakeDamage(int)'
fixes: Change line 12 to `public void TakeDamage(int amount) { }`
steps.hint: Compare the interface's method with the one in `Crate`, parameter by parameter.
steps.explanation: The interface promises `TakeDamage(int amount)`, but `Crate` has a `TakeDamage()` with no parameter, which is a different method, so the promise isn't kept (CS0535). Matching the parameter fixes it. Changing the call doesn't fix the class; an interface member must be implemented as `public` (CS0737); and without `: IDamageable`, a `Crate` can't be stored in an `IDamageable` variable.

steps.title: Enums: a fixed set of names

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: The names are numbered 0, 1, 2. What does `++` do to a number?
steps.explanation: `Calm` is 0, so `mood++` makes it 1, which is **Alert**, and printing an enum shows the name. `(int)Mood.Angry` reveals the number behind it, **2**. And `mood` is now `Mood.Alert`, so the comparison is **True**.

steps.prompt: Base class or interface? Sort each design need.

items.text: Slime and Bat share the same movement code from Enemy
Every enemy has health and a Die() method written once
A Boss is an Enemy but overrides Attack()
Crates, players and doors can all take damage
Anything the player can interact with by pressing E
Things that can be saved to a file

steps.explanation: Use a **base class** when the types really are one kind of thing and share code. Use an **interface** when unrelated types share a *capability*: a crate and a player have little in common except that both can take damage. Since a class can implement many interfaces, they also mix freely.

lessons.title: Records and pattern matching
lessons.takeaway: A one-line `record` gives you an immutable data type that compares by value, and switch expressions with patterns test types, properties and ranges in one readable block.

steps.title: Records: data in one line

steps.prompt: `Card` is a record and `Chip` is an ordinary class with the same data. What does this print?
steps.hint: For a class, `==` asks "same object?". For a record it asks "same values?".
steps.explanation: The two cards have the same values, so `a == b` is **True**. For a class, `==` compares references, and `x` and `y` are two different objects: **False**. `a with { Value = 11 }` is a new card with only `Value` changed, and a record prints its properties: **Card { Name = Ace, Value = 11 }**.

steps.title: Pattern matching

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: For each shape, go down the arms and stop at the first one that matches.
steps.explanation: The circle matches `Circle c`: **circle r=1**. `Square(2)` fails `{ Side: > 5 }` and falls to `Square q`: **square 2**. `Square(10)` matches the property pattern first: **big square**. If the `Square q` arm came before the property pattern, it would catch every square, and the compiler would reject the unreachable arm.

steps.prompt: `Grade(95)` should print `top`, but this doesn't compile. Click a line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS8510: The pattern is unreachable. It has already been handled by a previous arm of the switch expression or it is impossible to match.
fixes: Swap lines 5 and 6, so `>= 90` is checked first
steps.hint: Which scores could ever reach the `>= 90` arm?
steps.explanation: Every score of 90 or more is also `>= 50`, so the first arm catches it and the `>= 90` arm can never run. C# rejects that (CS8510). Put the narrower test first. `> 90` is just as unreachable. Changing or deleting the `_` arm leaves the real problem, the order of the first two arms, untouched, so the same error remains.

steps.prompt: Which of these is the best fit for a `record`?
choices: A high-score entry: a name, a score and a date that never change
The player, whose health and position change every frame
A level loader that reads files and keeps a cache
An audio mixer that many objects share and adjust
steps.explanation: Records shine for small, immutable pieces of data that are equal when their values are equal: two high-score entries with the same name, score and date are the same entry. A player, a loader and a mixer are things with identity and changing state, so they're classes.

units.title: Safe and reactive code
units.description: Handle missing values and failures without crashing, and let objects announce what happened.

lessons.title: null and nullable types
lessons.takeaway: `string?` may be null and `string` may not; before using a maybe-null value, check it or use `?.` (stop if null) and `??` (fallback if null).

steps.title: null means "no object"
steps.body:
A reference-type variable can hold **`null`**: no object at all. Using a member of `null`, like `.Length`, crashes with a `NullReferenceException`, the most common bug in C# programs.

Modern C# fights it with **nullable reference types**, switched on in every new project: `string` promises never to be null, and **`string?`** says it might be. The compiler tracks this and warns you *before* the program runs.

```csharp
string name = "Ana";        // can never be null
string? nickname = null;    // the ? says: this one might be null

Console.WriteLine(name.Length);           // 3
if (nickname != null)
{
    Console.WriteLine(nickname.Length);   // safe: inside this if, it can't be null
}

int? bonus = null;          // a value type needs ? to be able to hold null at all
Console.WriteLine(bonus.HasValue);        // False
```

steps.prompt: Ben has no nickname, so this should print `NO NICKNAME`. The compiler warns, and running it crashes. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
warning CS8602: Dereference of a possibly null reference.
Unhandled exception. System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object.
  ...
steps.hint: `FindNickname` returns `string?`. What happens when you call `.ToUpper()` on null?
steps.explanation: `nickname` is null for Ben, so `nickname.ToUpper()` throws, which is exactly what warning **CS8602** predicted. `?.` stops and gives null instead of calling `ToUpper`, and `??` replaces that null with the fallback. Declaring it as `string` just moves the warning (CS8600) and still crashes; `!` tells the compiler "trust me, it isn't null", which silences the warning but still crashes; and the `??` comes too late when `ToUpper` has already crashed.

steps.title: ?. and ??
steps.body:
Three short operators handle maybe-null values:

```csharp
string? city = null;

int? length = city?.Length;          // null, because city is null: no crash
string shown = city ?? "unknown";    // the fallback, used when the left side is null
city ??= "Lisbon";                   // assign only if city is still null

Console.WriteLine(length == null);   // True
Console.WriteLine(shown);            // unknown
Console.WriteLine(city);             // Lisbon
```

- `a?.B`: if `a` is null, the result is null; otherwise it's `a.B`
- `x ?? y`: `x`, unless it's null, then `y`
- `x ??= y`: set `x` to `y` only if `x` is null

They chain: `player?.Guild?.Name ?? "none"` survives a missing player *and* a missing guild.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: `a?.Length` is null when `a` is null, and `??` then supplies -1.
steps.explanation: `a` is null, so `a?.Length` is null and `?? -1` gives **-1**. `b` is `"hi"`, so `b?.Length` is **2** and the fallback isn't used. `a ??= "set"` assigns because `a` is still null, so the last line prints **set**.

steps.title: A chain of maybes
steps.problem: A `Player?` may be missing, and a player's `Guild?` may be missing too. Write `GuildName(Player? p)` that returns the guild's name or `"no guild"`, without any `if`. What does it give for a player in the Owls guild, a player with no guild, and `null`?
steps: Start from `p`, which may be null: `p?.Guild` is null if there's no player, else the player's guild (which may itself be null).
Go one more step with another `?.`: `p?.Guild?.Name` is null if either link is missing.
Supply the fallback once, at the end: `p?.Guild?.Name ?? "no guild"`.
steps.answer: `string GuildName(Player? p) => p?.Guild?.Name ?? "no guild";` gives `Owls`, `no guild` and `no guild`. The first missing link short-circuits the rest of the chain.

steps.prompt: In a project with nullable reference types switched on, which of these variables may hold `null`?

items.text: `string? title`
`int? score`
`Player? target`
`string title`
`int score`
`bool done`
`List<string> names`

steps.hint: Look for the `?`.
steps.explanation: The `?` is what allows null. For value types it's a hard rule: `int score = null` doesn't compile (CS0037). For reference types such as `string` and `List<string>` it's the compiler's promise: assigning null to one gives warning CS8600, and the compiler then trusts that it's never null.

steps.hint: Arithmetic with a null `int?` gives null.
steps.explanation: `bonus ?? 5` is 5, so `score` is 15. `10 + bonus` with a null `bonus` is **null** (not 10), so `total ?? 100` is 100. 15 + 100 = **115**.

lessons.title: Exceptions: when things go wrong
lessons.takeaway: An exception jumps to the nearest matching `catch` (most specific first) and `finally` always runs; for input that's often bad, use `TryParse` instead of catching.

steps.title: try, catch, finally

steps.prompt: `int.Parse` throws a `FormatException` when the text isn't a whole number. What does this print?
steps.hint: After the exception, does the rest of the `try` block still run?
steps.explanation: `A` prints, then `int.Parse("12x")` throws, so `B` is **skipped**. The `FormatException` catch prints `C`, `finally` prints `D`, and since the exception was handled the program continues with `E`.

steps.title: Expected problems aren't exceptional

steps.prompt: When the user types something that isn't a number, this should print `please type a number`. It crashes instead. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error:
Unhandled exception. System.FormatException: The input string 'seven' was not in a correct format.
  ...
fixes: Change line 2 to `int.TryParse(input, out int count);`
steps.hint: Which method copes with text that isn't a number, without throwing?
steps.explanation: `int.Parse("seven")` throws a `FormatException`. `int.TryParse` returns false instead and sets `count` to 0, so line 3 prints the message. (In real code, use the `bool` it returns: `if (int.TryParse(...))`.) A string can't be cast to an `int` (CS0030), `Convert.ToInt32` throws the same `FormatException`, and marking the input as nullable changes nothing about its text.

steps.prompt: This should print `no such slot`, but it doesn't compile. Click a line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0160: A previous catch clause already catches all exceptions of this or of a super type ('Exception')
steps.hint: Every exception type is a kind of `Exception`. Which `catch` gets the first chance?
steps.explanation: `catch` blocks are tried top to bottom. `catch (Exception)` matches **every** exception, so the specific block after it could never run, and C# rejects it (CS0160). Put specific exceptions first and general ones last. Naming the variable changes nothing; deleting the specific block compiles but prints `something failed`; and a bare `catch` catches everything too, so the same problem remains.

steps.title: Choosing what to throw
steps.problem: A `Wallet` holds 30 coins. `Withdraw(amount)` must reject amounts of zero or less and refuse to go below zero. Which exception fits each case, and what happens for -5, 50 and 20 when the caller catches both?
steps: A negative amount is a bad **argument**: `throw new ArgumentException("amount must be positive");`
50 is a valid amount, but the wallet's current state can't allow it: `throw new InvalidOperationException("not enough money");`
The caller wraps each call in `try` with one `catch` per type and reports the exception's `Message`.
-5 is caught as a bad amount, 50 is refused, and 20 succeeds, leaving 10.
steps.answer: `bad amount: amount must be positive`, `refused: not enough money`, `ok, 10 left`. Choosing a specific exception type lets callers handle each failure differently.

steps.hint: Which strings are whole numbers? An empty string isn't.
steps.explanation: "4", "10" and "-3" parse, so `sum` is 4 + 10 - 3 = **11**. "x" and the empty string "" throw `FormatException`, which is caught, so the loop prints a `skipped` line for each and carries on.

lessons.title: Delegates and events
lessons.takeaway: A delegate holds methods to call later; an event exposes one so others can subscribe with `+=` and unsubscribe with `-=`, while only the owner can raise it with `?.Invoke(...)`.

steps.title: Delegates: methods in a variable
steps.body:
`Func` and `Action` from the LINQ lesson are **delegates**: types for "a method with this shape". A delegate variable can hold a named method or a lambda, and `+=` adds more methods, which are then all called in order:

```csharp
Func<int, int> op = Double;    // a delegate variable can hold a named method...
Console.WriteLine(op(5));      // 10
op = x => x + 100;             // ...or a lambda of the same shape
Console.WriteLine(op(5));      // 105

Action greet = () => Console.WriteLine("hi");
greet += () => Console.WriteLine("there");   // += adds another method to call
greet();                       // hi, then there

int Double(int x) => x * 2;
```

This is how code says "call this later": a button that runs something when clicked, a timer that runs something when it ends.

steps.prompt: `onScore` holds two lambdas. What does this print?
steps.hint: Both lambdas run on every call, in the order they were added. The first one updates `total`.
steps.explanation: Each call runs the first lambda (which adds to `total`) and then the second (which prints). So `onScore(5)` prints **+5 (total 5)** and `onScore(3)` prints **+3 (total 8)**. The lambdas can use and change `total` from the surrounding code.

steps.title: Events

steps.prompt: This should print `+10`, but it doesn't compile. Click the line with the bug.
steps.error: error CS0070: The event 'Game.Scored' can only appear on the left hand side of += or -= (except when used from within the type 'Game')
fixes: Change line 8 to `public void AddPoints(int pts) => Scored(pts);`
steps.hint: From outside `Game`, what are the only two things you can do with `Scored`?
steps.explanation: Outside its class, an event may only appear on the left of `+=` or `-=` (CS0070), so code outside `Game` can't raise it. Ask the owner to do it through `AddPoints`. `?.Invoke` is still raising it from outside; `=` would replace everyone's subscriptions, which events forbid too; and changing line 8 leaves line 3 broken.

steps.prompt: What does this print?
steps.hint: `-=` removes the exact delegate stored in `creak`.
steps.explanation: The first `Open()` runs both subscribers: **creak**, **light on**. Then `-= creak` removes the creak handler, so the second `Open()` prints only **light on**. This only works because the lambda was kept in a variable: `-=` with a brand-new lambda, even an identical-looking one, would remove nothing.

steps.prompt: A health bar listens to a player's `HealthChanged` event. Put the steps in the order they happen.
items: An enemy hits the player, and the player's `TakeDamage` lowers its health
`UpdateBar` runs with the new health value
steps.explanation: Subscribing has to happen first, or nobody is listening. When something changes, the owner raises the event and every subscriber runs **right then**, one after another; only after they've all finished does `Invoke` return and the owner's method carry on.
